questions.stem: Which type of radiation does the surface of the Earth re-emit after absorbing sunlight?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Ultraviolet arrives from the sun; the surface emits infrared.
Gamma rays play no role in the greenhouse process.
Radio waves are not part of this heat exchange.

questions.stem: Which gases absorb the re-emitted heat?

options.explanation: Ground ozone is not the named trapping gas set.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour — the greenhouse gases
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The bulk atmosphere does not trap this heat; greenhouse gases do.
Argon absorbs essentially none of it.

questions.stem: What fraction of the re-emitted heat escapes to space?

options.explanation: Part of the heat does reflect back into space.
All surface heat behaves the same way.

options.text: Some escapes, while the rest is trapped by greenhouse gases
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
If all escaped, the Earth would freeze.

questions.stem: Why is the greenhouse effect described as essential?

options.explanation: Rainfall depends on the water cycle, not directly on this trapping.
Sunlight passes through; heat is what gets trapped.
Light powers photosynthesis, not trapped heat.

options.text: Because it keeps the planet warm enough for life to survive
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Put the greenhouse sequence in the correct order.

options.text: Solar radiation enters, the surface absorbs and re-emits heat, gases trap part of it
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Gases trap sunlight before it lands
options.explanation: Gases trap outgoing heat, not incoming light.
Absorption happens first, then re-emission.

options.text: Heat leaves before it is trapped
options.explanation: Trapping follows re-emission.

questions.stem: State what the greenhouse effect is.
questions.modelAnswer: The greenhouse effect is the natural trapping of heat in the atmosphere of the Earth by greenhouse gases.

questions.stem: Name three greenhouse gases that trap heat in the atmosphere.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are greenhouse gases that absorb and trap heat.

questions.stem: Explain why the planet would freeze without greenhouse gases.
questions.modelAnswer: Without greenhouse gases, re-emitted heat would escape to space unchecked, so the surface would lose warmth and drop below the level that supports life.

questions.stem: On a cloudless desert night, temperature drops sharply. Link to the mechanism.
questions.modelAnswer: Dry, cloudless air holds little water vapour, so less re-emitted heat is trapped and the desert surface cools quickly overnight.

questions.stem: What turns a natural greenhouse effect into an enhanced one?

options.explanation: Enhancement means more trapping, not less.

options.text: Human activities raising the levels of greenhouse gases
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Volcanic activity cools the planet; enhancement comes from gases.
Solar weakening would cool, not warm, the surface.

questions.stem: Which human activities add greenhouse gases to the atmosphere?

options.explanation: Recycling reduces emissions; it does not raise them.
Wind generation displaces fossil burning.

options.text: Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Trees absorb carbon dioxide; they do not add it.
The term tracks the average, not single days.
The poles are warming fastest, not cooling.
The term is global, not about glasshouses.

options.text: The average temperature of the Earth rising above its normal level
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which chain of ocean consequences follows warming?

options.text: Warmer oceans melt polar ice, raising sea levels and causing flooding and coral bleaching
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Warming, not cooling, drives the named effects.
Sea levels rise with meltwater in the account.
Size changes are not the documented consequence.

questions.stem: Why does biodiversity fall as warming proceeds?

options.text: Because biodiversity is fixed by latitude
options.explanation: It shifts with habitat loss and disruption.

options.text: Because disrupted food chains and rising extinction rates remove species
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Resilience falls; the account points to disruption and extinction.

options.text: Because all species move to cities
options.explanation: Species migrate to new habitats, not cities.

questions.stem: State what causes the enhanced greenhouse effect.
questions.modelAnswer: The enhanced greenhouse effect is caused by increasing levels of greenhouse gases released through human activities.

questions.stem: Name two consequences of global warming for the oceans.
questions.modelAnswer: Ocean temperatures increase, melting polar ice caps and raising sea levels, and warmer water stresses corals, causing bleaching.

questions.stem: Explain why deforestation feeds the enhanced greenhouse effect.
questions.modelAnswer: Deforestation removes trees that absorbed carbon dioxide, so less carbon is locked away while the cleared material often releases more when burned.

questions.stem: A coastal village floods more often than a decade ago. Give the warming link.
questions.modelAnswer: Warming raises ocean temperatures and melts polar ice, so sea levels climb and low-lying coastal villages flood more frequently.
